mcqs.question: Why can't application code just connect to a backend Pod's IP directly?
options: Pod IPs are encrypted and unreadable by other Pods
Pod IPs change whenever a Pod is rescheduled, so a hardcoded IP breaks
Kubernetes doesn't allow Pod-to-Pod traffic at all
Pods don't have IP addresses, only Services do
mcqs.explanation: Pods are ephemeral: a crash or reschedule gets a new IP. Services exist precisely to give a stable address in front of that churn. Pods do have real IPs and can normally reach each other directly — the problem is stability, not encryption or connectivity being blocked.

mcqs.question: Which Service type is the right default for exposing a production web app to the public internet on a cloud provider?
options: ClusterIP
NodePort
LoadBalancer
ExternalName
mcqs.explanation: LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer with a stable public IP/DNS and is the standard way to expose a service externally in production. ClusterIP is internal-only, NodePort is a manual/dev-oriented high-port mechanism, and ExternalName just aliases to an external DNS name without proxying traffic.

mcqs.question: What does an Ingress object do without an Ingress controller installed in the cluster?
options: It routes traffic using a built-in default proxy
Nothing — it's inert configuration until a controller reads and acts on it
It automatically provisions a cloud load balancer itself
It falls back to NodePort routing
mcqs.explanation: Ingress is just an API object describing desired routing rules. Nothing in the cluster acts on it unless an Ingress controller — a Pod running an actual proxy — is deployed to watch and implement those rules. There is no built-in default proxy or automatic fallback.

mcqs.question: Once a Pod is selected by any NetworkPolicy, what's the default behavior for traffic not explicitly allowed?
options: It's allowed, since NetworkPolicies only add extra permissions
It's denied — NetworkPolicies are allow-list only, so anything not permitted is blocked
It depends on the Pod's resource limits
It's logged but still allowed through
mcqs.explanation: NetworkPolicies work as an allow-list: as soon as a Pod matches any policy's selector, traffic to/from it is denied by default except what a rule explicitly permits. This is a common trip-up for people expecting policies to be purely additive on top of an already-open default.

mcqs.question: You've applied a NetworkPolicy restricting traffic to a database Pod, but traffic from disallowed Pods still gets through. What's the most likely cause?
options: NetworkPolicies take up to 24 hours to take effect
The cluster's CNI plugin doesn't implement NetworkPolicy enforcement
NetworkPolicies only apply to Ingress traffic, never Pod-to-Pod
The policy needs a corresponding Service to work
mcqs.explanation: NetworkPolicy enforcement is delegated to the CNI plugin — if it doesn't implement policy enforcement, the object is accepted by the API server but has zero effect on actual traffic. There's no propagation delay of that scale, no Service dependency, and it does apply to Pod-to-Pod (east-west) traffic, which is its main purpose.
